title: LLM Active Alignment: A Nash Equilibrium Perspective
claim: Exclusion of some groups emerges across models and datasets in distinct regions of preference-coefficient space, not just in one setting.
layout: 6 panels in 2x3 grid, heatmaps with shared colorbars, captions below
description: A 2x3 grid of heatmaps. Each shows one focal subpopulation's interior Nash-equilibrium weight over two preference coefficients, beta(A), beta(I) or beta(D). Both axes are log-scaled from 1e-4 to 1e4. A colorbar from about 0.05 to 0.35 runs from magenta/crimson through tan to gray-blue and off-white. Black regions mark political exclusion, where weight is below 0.05. White regions mark parameter values with no interior equilibrium. The black areas take different shapes: a top-left wedge, a small bottom-left corner, a top horizontal band, a diagonal strip, a large bottom-left block, and a vertical strip. Each panel has a caption below giving the model (Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Mistral-7B), the dataset (Big Five Personality, CultureBank, POLITICS) and the subpopulation (for example Neuroticism or Reddit-Left). The eye goes first to the black exclusion regions.
caption: Representative examples of political exclusion across models and datasets (complete results in Appx. [ref]). Each panel fixes the base model, dataset, and subpopulation, and visualizes the subpopulation’s interior Nash-equilibrium weight under varying preference coefficients. Specifically, one coefficient among $\beta^{(A)}$, $\beta^{(I)}$, and $\beta^{(D)}$ is fixed to $1$, while the remaining two vary along the x- and y-axes (as labeled, log-scaled). Color indicates the resulting equilibrium weight assigned to the focal subpopulation. Regions where the weight falls below $0.05$ are marked in black and referred to as the political exclusion area. White regions indicate parameter values for which no interior equilibrium exists. We focus on interior equilibria because boundary equilibria necessarily set at least one subpopulation weight to zero and our goal is to understand how to avoid political exclusion.
abstract: We develop a game-theoretic framework for predicting and steering the behavior of populations of large language models (LLMs) through Nash equilibrium (NE) analysis. To avoid the intractability of equilibrium computation in open-ended text spaces, we model each agent's action as a mixture over human subpopulations. Agents choose actively and strategically which groups to align with, yielding an interpretable and behaviorally substantive policy class. We derive closed-form NE characterizations, adopting standard concave-utility assumptions to enable analytical system-level predictions and give explicit, actionable guidance for shifting alignment targets toward socially desirable outcomes. The method functions as an active alignment layer on top of existing alignment pipelines such as RLHF. In a social-media setting, we show that a population of LLMs, especially reasoning-based models, may exhibit political exclusion, pathologies where some subpopulations are ignored by all LLM agents, which can be avoided by our method, illustrating the promise of applying the method to regulate multi-agent LLM dynamics across domains.
